about: What NuclearLang and Synapsis are for: the problem, the idea, the advantages and how it works. What a person asks first.

rows.title: What NuclearLang is
rows.summary: NuclearLang (Nuclear, `.nuc` files) is a minimal language made for AI agents and the people who work with them: you write only the logic of a program, with the fewest tokens, and a transpiler turns it into the code of another technology (TypeScript, Dart, Python) through dialects.
body: NuclearLang is a small base language. A file ends in `.nuc`. It is not compiled to machine code: a transpiler written in Rust turns `.nuc` into the code of another technology. It goes one way only: `.nuc` → `.ts`, `.dart` or `.py`. It never reads target code.

The idea in one line: write the business logic of the product, and leave everything else to the framework and the transpiler. The wiring of a framework, imports, serialization, state and tests are always the same, so you do not write them.
It has three parts that work together:
- **The base language**: indentation instead of braces, `~` to await, `Result<E, T>` for errors, one standard library of its own. One way to write each thing.
- **Dialects**: data files (TOML and templates) loaded at run time that say how Nuclear is written in a target. A dialect is added without changing the compiler.
- **Synapsis**: the framework. Three platforms (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`), each written once in Nuclear and built by its dialects (`fastapi`, `nestjs`, `flutter`, `react`).

Around it there is a full toolchain: one command line, `nuclear`, a language server, extensions for VS Code, Android Studio and Zed, a private knowledge base (the Nuclear Smart Graph), an MCP server (`nuclear-mcp`), local AI agents (the Nuclear Developer) and a pipeline from a spec to deployed code (the Builder, `nuclear-builder`).
It is open source (Apache-2.0), in the spirit of Rust, Deno, Gleam and Bun.

rows.title: Why NuclearLang exists: the problem it solves
rows.summary: An AI agent that writes an application spends most of its tokens on code that is always the same (the wiring of a framework, imports, serialization, state, tests), invents APIs that do not exist, and people read and review all of it. In Nuclear only the business logic is written; the framework brings the architecture and the transpiler writes the rest.
body: The problem:
- **Agents pay for text that is not logic.** Most of the tokens of an application go to code that is always the same: the wiring of a framework, imports, serialization, state, tests.
- **Agents invent APIs** that do not exist.
- **People read and review all of it.**
What NuclearLang does about it:
- You write **only the business logic**, with one way to write each thing and the fewest tokens.
- The **framework brings the architecture** (Synapsis): three platforms, `web`, `mobile` and `backend`, written once in Nuclear, so the wiring is not written by hand.
- The **compiler answers with exact fixes**: every error has a code, a position and the fix, as text or JSON, so an agent repairs its own code.
- **Type definitions**, so nobody invents an API.
- The **same Nuclear builds with every dialect of its platform**: a backend written once comes out as a Python (`fastapi`) or a TypeScript (`nestjs`) service.
What it leaves out on purpose: it never reads or converts target code into Nuclear, it does not replace the target's own tools, and it has no package manager of its own.

Because the language is small and regular, a local model of at most 3B parameters with the right knowledge base writes it well: the local developer passes 43 of 45 tasks of its evaluation, where Claude Sonnet passes 39 (`concept:nuclear-developer`).

rows.title: The advantages of NuclearLang and Synapsis
rows.summary: Fewer tokens and less text, one way to write each thing, errors that come with their fix, the framework generated for you, one code for several target technologies, local AI agents that work on your machine, and generated code as fast as an expert's.
body: **For an AI agent**
- Few tokens: only the logic is written. No imports, no wiring, no boilerplate.
- One way to write each thing, so there is less to guess and less to get wrong.
- Diagnostics with a code, a position and usually the exact `fix` (`nuclear check --json`, `nuclear fix`): the agent repairs its code by itself.
- Type definitions of the target's libraries: an invented class or argument is an error with "did you mean", not a bug found at run time.
- Generators write the standard code of a feature, finished and compiling (`nuclear gen resource`), so the agent writes only what is special.
**For a developer**
- You write business logic; Synapsis writes dependency injection, routing, JSON, validation, state classes and tests.
- The same architecture in every project and on every platform: components, use cases, repositories, one facade per component. The compiler enforces it.
- One CLI builds, runs, tests, migrates and repairs the project (`synapsis`).
- Editor support like a native language: completion, hover, rename, debugging of `.nuc` lines, devices, an HTTP client.
- A backend publishes its contract and its apps get their models and repositories generated: a renamed field breaks the build, not the phone.
**For a team**
- One code, several technologies: the Nuclear of a platform never changes when its dialect changes (a backend builds as FastAPI or as NestJS).
- The generated code is the code an expert would write in the target, and it passes the target's strict analyzer (`tsc --strict`, `flutter analyze`, `pyright --strict`).
- Transpiling is instant: a project builds in about 20 ms; a build with no changes takes about 40 ms.
- AI that runs on your machine: local agents of at most 3B parameters, a private knowledge base and no code sent anywhere unless you choose a frontier model to lead.
- Open source, Apache-2.0.

**What is measured.** On the evaluation the local 3B coder passes every task of one file (42 of 42; Claude Sonnet passes 36). In the benchmark of generated code against hand-written code the output is identical and the slowest generated program takes 1.11 times the hand-written one.

rows.title: How NuclearLang works: from a .nuc file to the target's code
rows.summary: The compiler reads `.nuc`, checks it and writes the target's code with a dialect: Rust decides what is emitted, the dialect (TOML and templates) decides how. A project is built as a whole, with its architecture rules.
body: 1. **Lexer and parser** read the `.nuc` file. The parser is the same for every dialect and never stops at the first error: it reports all of them at once.
2. **The resolver** checks names, scopes, `Result` handling and the standard library. Every problem is a diagnostic with a code (`N0106`), a position and often the exact fix.

3. **The dialect** is loaded at run time: a folder of data (`dialect.toml`, templates, `docs.toml`). It says how each construct, kind and decorator is written in the target, which imports a name needs and which packages the project carries.
4. **The emitter** writes the target's code. Rust decides *what* is emitted; the dialect decides *how*. The output is what an expert would write in that target.

5. **A project** (a folder with `config.nuc`) is built as a whole: one build, imports between files written for you, the architecture rules of its platform checked, and its manifest, tests and wiring generated in `build/`.
Things that follow from this design:
- It is one way only: `.nuc` → target. Nuclear never reads TypeScript, Dart or Python.
- Dialects inherit: `nestjs` extends `nodejs`, which extends `typescript`. A platform dialect (`fastapi`) adds a framework to a language dialect (`python`).
- A new target or framework is a new dialect: data files, never a change in the compiler.
- The generated code is never edited: change the `.nuc` and build again.
The commands: `nuclear check` (errors), `nuclear build` (transpile), `nuclear fix` (apply the exact fixes), `nuclear fmt` (canonical layout); for a Synapsis project, `nuclear build | run | test`.

rows.title: The golden rule: performance, speed and readability of the syntax
rows.summary: Every decision of the base language and of every dialect must keep three things: generated code as fast as an expert's, instant transpilation, and minimal, readable Nuclear. A rule, kind or shortcut that breaks one of the three is rejected.
body: The golden rule governs the language and every dialect (ADR-lang-0001):

- **Performance**: the generated code is as fast as what an expert writes in the target. No runtime layer between Nuclear and the target: a property is a property, a method is the target's method or a one-line helper.
- **Speed**: transpiling is instant, because the compiler reads only what it needs.
- **Readability**: Nuclear stays minimal. One way to write each thing; explicit beats implicit when in doubt; errors over magic.

Two more rules come with it. Quality first: the right solution, even when it costs more, never a shortcut that bends a rule. And the parser never changes for a dialect: framework words live in the dialects.

rows.title: A product is made with the tools, never by porting code by hand
rows.summary: A product (any software made from Nuclear: an app, a backend, the website, an example) is made with the platform's tools: `nuclear new`, `gen`, `make`, the MCP server, `nuclear add` for a library, `nuclear fix`. No agent writes target code (TypeScript, Dart, Python) for a feature, and no agent translates React, Node.js, Python or Dart code into Nuclear by hand.
body: Every product is a test of the platform: if an agent writes a feature by hand in the target's language, or ports native code into Nuclear by itself, nobody learns whether the tools would have made it.
1. The code is Nuclear; the target code comes from the transpiler. Never edit `build/`.
2. The standard parts come from the generators (`nuclear gen resource`, `nuclear gen usecase`, `nuclear make <kind>`) and the MCP server's tools.
3. A library is added with `nuclear add <package>` and used through its generated type definitions.
4. Only what the tools leave is written by hand, in Nuclear.

5. By hand outside Nuclear only when strictly necessary (the product cannot work otherwise, or the work is on Nuclear itself): say so, and the missing capability goes to the roadmap of the tool that should have done it.

rows.title: Who NuclearLang is for
rows.summary: For AI coding agents (few tokens, one way to write, fixes in the errors), for developers of apps and backends (only business logic, one CLI, native editor support) and for dialect authors (a new target without touching the compiler).
body: - **AI coding agents** (Claude, Codex, OpenCode, a local model): few tokens, one way to write each thing, diagnostics with fixes, a short sheet to follow (`nuclear spec --brief`), type definitions so they do not invent APIs, an MCP server with every tool.
- **Developers of apps and backends**: they write business logic only; one CLI builds, tests and runs the project; the editor works like a native one.
- **Dialect authors**: they add a target language or a framework with data files, templates and tests, never with Rust.

It is a good fit when the product is a mobile app, a web app or an HTTP backend with data, events or AI agents, and when part of the work is done by AI agents. It is not a fit when the goal is to convert existing TypeScript, Dart or Python into Nuclear: it does not read target code.

rows.title: What NuclearLang does not try to do
rows.summary: It does not read or convert target code into Nuclear, it does not replace the platform's own tools (Flutter still builds and runs the app), and it leaves out features that cannot be written the same in every target.
body: - **No reverse direction.** Nuclear never reads or converts TypeScript, Dart or Python into `.nuc`.
- **No replacement of the platform's tools.** Flutter's CLI still builds and runs a mobile app, `uvicorn` or `npm` still serve a backend; Synapsis drives them.
- **No feature that only one target has.** Records, operator overloading and Dart 3 pattern `switch` are not part of the language.
- **No magic.** No inferred parameters, no hoisting: when in doubt, explicit wins and the compiler says what is missing.
asks: can nuclear convert my existing code

rows.title: NuclearLang compared with writing the framework by hand, with generators and with low-code
rows.summary: By hand you write and maintain the framework's ceremony; a framework's generator writes it once and then it is yours to maintain; low-code hides the code. Nuclear keeps the logic as code you own and regenerates the rest on every build.
body: **Against writing Flutter, NestJS or FastAPI by hand.** By hand, each feature is its logic plus imports, annotations, registration, serializers, state classes and tests wired to the framework. In Nuclear the same feature is its logic; the rest is generated on every build, the same way in every project. The generated code is what an expert writes, so nothing is lost at run time.

**Against a framework's generators** (Rails scaffolds, `phx.gen`, `artisan make`, `nest g`). Those write files once; from then on the boilerplate is yours to read and keep in step. In Nuclear the boilerplate is never in your sources: it lives in `build/` and is written again each time. `nuclear gen` also writes finished Nuclear from a resource's data, but what it writes is logic-level code, short enough to read.

**Against a cross-platform language** (Kotlin Multiplatform, Dart everywhere). Those run one runtime everywhere. Nuclear has no runtime of its own: each platform gets the native stack of its target (Flutter for mobile, React for web, FastAPI or NestJS for a backend).
**Against low-code.** Low-code hides the program. Nuclear is code: text files, version control, tests, a compiler, and generated sources you can read.

**The honest part.** For plain algorithms the base language is about as long as the target (the benchmark's two CPU programs: 1.03 and 0.84 times the hand-written lines). The saving is in the framework kinds, where a few lines of Nuclear become several files of the target.
asks: how is nuclear different from flutter
